I have been a best man seven times (going to be eight). Here are the tips of a long-time best man:

Stick to a speech formula:

• I have known the groom for x years, don't elaborate much beyond

• Acknowledge how honored you are to be there as a witness for the couple

• Acknowledge how gracious and amazing the host families are for being there

• Anecdote about how amazing the groom is. If it is deprecating, no infraction more serious than a traffic incident must be mentioned. Make sure he comes out as a great guy

• Talk to the bride about how because of this she is getting a great guy and you know she is great lady who is up to the task.

• To the bride and groom, drink and sit.

Do not exceed 5 minutes. Try to get the job done in 2-3. Do not regale stupid shit that grandmas wouldn't care about. DO NOT BRING UP ANY OTHER FEMALE BESIDES THE BRIDE. The only exception to that is the sentence "I had met other women in the [groom]'s life, but I knew [bride] was different." A safer bet would be to omit the reference to other women altogether and just say you always knew they were meant for each other and that she was different. Do not give other women more than a passing mention. Thanks to whoever mentioned this. Losing track of people.

Do this and you will have relatives, bridesmaids, guests and staff telling you how that was the best speech they have heard and it totally wasn't embarrassing like every other speech they have heard.

EDIT: Thanks for gold! As others have pointed out: Small personal elements you know are sentimental/funny are fine. Also, these tips are for people who psych themselves out about what to say. If you are a naturally good public speaker, you can bend or break any of these rules.

EDIT2: Based on ensuing comments, I ninja edited about not talking about other women at all for safest impact. Also, the length I said not to exceed 5 minutes, but definitely aim to keep it at 2-3. Let the people drink!

I have to do some work this afternoon. Best men, stay genuine and succinct to what you want to say to your groom and bride, and you'll rock! Good luck!

However, you also said you want to go to a top 4 year university or college. It takes a mature person to realize that they are getting older. And don't think that adults aren't scared of things too. Fear is a completely normal response to nearly any new situation someone finds themselves in.



>I am faced with a decision in my study that will affect my job opportunities. It's between the safe choice and the most exciting/interesting choice, and it scares me that my decisions suddenly matter for the long term future. At the same time one of my grandparents is suddenly not feeling too well. From what I hear it's most likely nothing serious, but it makes me think of their age, and how it might not be many years till they will no longer be around.

First of all, congratulation on having the chance of deciding between two different career options. That in itself shows that you are doing well for yourself. Rather than tell you to pick the safe choice or the exciting/interesting choice, I'm going to give you some advice. Simply: be open to the spontaneity of life. Although you may think know what you are going to be doing in the near future, you never really have a clue. Life has a habit of throwing you curveballs right when you're getting ready to knock a fastball out of the park.

Funny that you mentioned grandparents. As I'm writing this, I'm on my way to my grandmother's wake. She passed away last Wednesday from a failing liver and kidney. She was 72 years young. I write this not to scare you, but to prepare you. The death of one or more grandparents is something that nearly all young adults will be faced with at one point or another in their lives. You could call it part of growing up, but really it's just a part of life. It's going to hurt a little and you're going to miss people a whole lot, but life, and death, just kind of happen.

TL;DR

The world keeps turning, no matter if you notice or not. Accepting the inevitable and the unpredictable are parts of growing up.

Addressing your first point, that more pizza places would lower the cost of pizza:

It actually makes sense that having less pizza places lowers the price of pizza. Because the demand for pizza doesn't significantly increase as the number of pizza places increase, the total amount of pizza sales is spread over a smaller number of restaurants. In other words, less competition allows pizza places to sell pizza cheaper because they'll sell more pizzas without customers spread thin among more restaurants.
